prompt: Why is encrypting stored passwords the wrong design?

choices.text: Encryption is too slow for a sign-in form
choices.why: Speed is not the problem; reversibility is.

choices.text: Whoever has the key reads them all back
choices.why: Right. And the key lives on the servers that hold the table.

choices.text: Encrypted values are longer than the column allows
choices.why: Columns are sized for what you store.

choices.text: The law forbids encrypting personal data
choices.why: It encourages it, for data that must be read back.

prompt: What does an attacker with a leaked table of SHA-256 hashes actually do?

choices.text: Reverses each hash with a mathematical formula
choices.why: SHA-256 is one-way; nobody reverses it.

choices.text: Asks the portal to decrypt them
choices.why: The portal holds nothing to decrypt.

choices.text: Hashes guesses and compares, billions a second
choices.why: Right. A fast hash makes guessing cheap.

choices.text: Nothing, because a hash cannot be used to sign in
choices.why: Finding the password that matches is enough.

prompt: Match each property of a password hash to what it buys.

pairs.right: graphics cards cannot run thousands at once

right_distractors: the password can be read back

prompt: Which are password hashing functions recommended today? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Argon2id
choices.why: OWASP lists it first.

choices.text: scrypt
choices.why: Second in OWASP's list.

choices.text: bcrypt
choices.why: Older, still sound.

choices.text: SHA-256
choices.why: A good hash for other jobs, and fast, which is the problem here.

prompt: A patient's password was `Vereda2026!`, and the table is stored with Argon2id. After a leak, is her password safe?

choices.text: Yes: Argon2id makes every password safe
choices.why: It makes guesses costly, not weak passwords strong.

choices.text: Not really: it is among the first guesses
choices.why: Right. Cost slows a search; a short, patterned password is found early in it.

choices.text: Yes, because the salt hides it
choices.why: The salt stops one guess serving two patients; it does not stop the guess.

choices.text: No, because Argon2id is reversible
choices.why: It is not.

choices.text: It was refused for lacking a capital letter

prompt: What does `@pytest.mark.parametrize` do in `test_app.py`?

choices.text: Runs the tests in parallel on four processor cores
choices.why: It repeats one test with different inputs, one after another.

choices.text: Marks the policy tests as optional
choices.why: They count like any other.

choices.text: Reads the passwords from a file
choices.why: They are written in the decorator.

choices.text: Runs one test once per pair of values
choices.why: Right. Each run is reported with the password in its name.

prompt: What does `$argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$…` carry besides the hash?

choices.text: The password, encrypted
choices.why: Nothing in it leads back to the password.

choices.text: The algorithm, its parameters and the salt
choices.why: Right. Everything needed to check a password later.

choices.text: The patient's name and the date the hash was made
choices.why: Neither is in it.

choices.text: A checksum of the database
choices.why: It describes one hash only.

prompt: Match each field of the PHC string to its meaning.
Why do parameters stored beside each hash make raising the cost safe?

choices.text: Argon2 ignores the parameters when it verifies
choices.why: It uses exactly those parameters.

choices.text: Raising the cost re-encrypts every password at once
choices.why: Nothing is re-encrypted; nothing could be.

choices.text: Old hashes still verify, and are upgraded at the next sign-in
choices.why: Right. check_needs_rehash is the line that does it.

choices.text: Patients are asked to choose a new password
choices.why: No patient has to do anything.

prompt: Why does the fixed portal verify an unknown name against a decoy hash?

choices.text: So a stranger's answer takes as long as a patient's
choices.why: Right. A faster answer for unknown names would reveal who is a patient.

choices.text: To let unknown names sign in with a shared password
choices.why: It returns False whatever the password.

choices.text: Argon2 needs a hash to start up
choices.why: It starts without one.

choices.text: To fill the USERS table with a placeholder row
choices.why: The decoy is never stored in USERS.

prompt: The first version answered `404 no such patient`. What did that tell a stranger?

choices.text: That the portal was down
choices.why: It was up and answering.

choices.text: The patient's password length
choices.why: Nothing about the password.

choices.text: Which clinic the patient visits
choices.why: The answer names no clinic.

choices.text: Whether a name belongs to a patient of Vereda
choices.why: Right. On a physiotherapy portal, that is a question about health.

prompt: bcrypt 5.0.0 refuses a password longer than how many bytes?
A wrong password makes `PasswordHasher.verify` raise `Verify___Error`.
What is the minimum length SP 800-63B asks for when a password is the only factor?

choices.text: 8 characters
choices.why: That is with a second factor.

choices.text: 15 characters
choices.why: Right, as on this portal.

choices.text: 64 characters, the maximum it allows
choices.why: 64 is what a site must at least accept, not require.

choices.text: 12 characters with a symbol
choices.why: No composition rules.

prompt: Which belong in a policy written to SP 800-63B? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: check against passwords from earlier breaches
choices.why: The blocklist.

choices.text: refuse the service's own name
choices.why: A context-specific word.

choices.text: allow pasting from a password manager
choices.why: Long random passwords depend on it.

choices.text: force a change every 90 days
choices.why: Only on evidence of compromise.

choices.text: require an uppercase letter and a symbol
choices.why: No composition rules.

prompt: Why are composition rules (upper case, digit, symbol) a weak policy?

choices.text: Symbols break the database's encoding
choices.why: Any encoding stores them.

choices.text: People meet them with the same few patterns
choices.why: Right. A capital, a year, an exclamation mark: tried first by every guessing tool.

choices.text: They make passwords too long to type on a phone
choices.why: They say nothing about length beyond eight.

choices.text: Argon2 cannot hash symbols
choices.why: It hashes any bytes.

prompt: A password that would be refused by the fixed policy for containing the company's name: `___@2026Vereda!`.
How can a blocklist check use an outside service without sending the password?

choices.text: It sends the password encrypted with the service's public key
choices.why: The service could still decrypt it.

choices.text: It sends the Argon2 hash
choices.why: Salted hashes cannot be compared across services.

choices.text: It sends only the first characters of a hash
choices.why: Right. The service answers with every match for that prefix, and the comparison happens locally.

choices.text: It sends the password's length and first letter
choices.why: Both leak information and identify nothing.

prompt: Why does a changed password end every other session of the account?

choices.text: Sessions store the old password and stop matching
choices.why: Sessions store no password.

choices.text: Whoever the patient wants out is likely signed in
choices.why: Right. Otherwise she believes she locked them out, and did not.

choices.text: To save memory on the server
choices.why: Not the reason.

choices.text: Flask requires it after set_password
choices.why: Flask knows nothing of it.

prompt: Why does the session that made the change stay valid?

choices.text: She is using it, and just proved the old password
choices.why: Right. Ending it would only make her sign in again.

choices.text: Ending the current session is impossible in Flask
choices.why: It is one line.

choices.text: It was created before the password changed
choices.why: So were the others that ended.

choices.text: Sessions on a laptop are trusted more than those on a phone
choices.why: The device is not the reason.

prompt: Why does the lesson prefer slowing answers over locking an account after failed sign-ins?

choices.text: Locking needs a database the portal lacks
choices.why: Storage is not the obstacle.

choices.text: Slowing is required by the LGPD
choices.why: The law does not say this.

choices.text: A lockout lets anybody lock any patient out
choices.why: Right. Failed attempts against a name are free to send.

choices.text: Locked accounts leak the password
choices.why: They do not.
